MI Agent, Medical Imaging Agent
LLMs, Harness, and Agents

Welcome to MIAgent Lab. MIAgent is a medical imaging agent that helps Codex or Claude tackle medical imaging challenges with human steering.

The design keeps the agent focused on one serious solution direction at a time, while leaving enough trace for humans to verify data, baselines, jobs, results, and next experiments.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

  • Explain the difference between an LLM model, an agent, and a harness.
  • Compare chatting with Qwen in Open WebUI with using an agent through OpenCode.
  • Describe the roles of Paseo and VS Code in the lab.
  • Locate the lab instructions, datasets, and experiment results.
  • Explain how the lab separates model serving, GPU training, and result tracking.

1. Concepts

1.1 Models, agents, and harnesses

In this section we'll explain to you what the difference is between a model, an agent, and a harness. You can simply ask your agent that question.

What's the difference between a model, an agent, and a harness? Can you explain to me with examples?
Expected output of the agent should be
Element What it is Other examples In this lab
LLM / model The model that predicts the next tokens. It generates responses and can propose tool calls, but does not execute commands itself. OpenAI GPT/coding models, Anthropic Claude, GLM from Z.ai, and Kimi from Moonshot AI. We use local Qwen, served by vLLM.
Harness The application around the model that manages the conversation and tool loop. It sends prompts and tool results to the model, exposes tools, and asks for the next action. Codex's harness, Claude Code, and Pi, a minimal coding harness. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent also contain runtime machinery around models. OpenCode is our harness. AGENTS.md and the MIAgent skills tell the agent how to work in this repository.
Agent The model plus instructions, tools, and a work loop. The agent can inspect files, run commands, record results, and decide what to try next. The model alone cannot do those things. Coding assistants such as Codex and Claude Code; personal-assistant applications such as OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. The agent uses Qwen, OpenCode, and the MIAgent instructions and tools to work on your task.

The distinction is the role: the model generates, the harness runs the model/tool loop, and the agent is the complete system working on a task. An agent product can also be described as a harness when discussing its underlying software. Claude is a model family; Claude Code is an agent application. Codex names OpenAI's coding-agent product, and also appears in some model names. Pi is harness software, not the Python language.

Two useful corollaries: 1- The same model behaves differently in different harnesses (opencode vs. a bare chat UI) because the tools and rules differ 2- The same harness can run different models. In this lab the harness is even layered — opencode is the LLM harness, while the MIAgent compose stack is the compute harness deciding where GPU work may run (which is exactly why the Lab 5 doc pins the container and launcher as "fixed facts").

2. Open the lab tools

We will explore the three concepts above using the same local Qwen model. First, use Open WebUI to see the model responding without tools. Then use Paseo or VS Code to interact with an agent: OpenCode supplies the harness, tools, and work loop around that model.

2.1 Open WebUI: chat with the model, without tools

On the landing page, click Open WebUI. It opens a new tab. Select the local Qwen model if a model is not already selected, then type a question.

This is the familiar experience of chatting with an LLM, like a conversation in ChatGPT: you send text and the model generates a reply. ChatGPT and other chat products can also offer search and other tools; those are additional capabilities, not something a language model can execute on its own.

For this exercise, Open WebUI is configured as model-only chat. Web search, code execution, external tool connections, image generation, and file tools are disabled. It cannot look up live information, inspect the MIAgent workspace, or run experiments. Its answers use its learned knowledge and the text in your conversation.

Open WebUI: a conversation with the local model, without the agent's tools.

Try a question the model can explain

Explain what a language model is in three sentences.
What is the difference between generating a command and executing it?
Expected output of the agent should be

Language model: A language model is a neural network trained to predict the next token (word piece) in a sequence, so it learns statistical patterns of language, reasoning, and code from large text corpora. By conditioning on prior context — including your instructions and tool outputs — it produces continuations that are coherent, task-relevant, and probabilistic rather than deterministic. It has no intrinsic access to the world: it only transforms text in to text out, which is why agents like me pair it with tools.

Generating vs. executing a command: Generating a command is me predicting text — a string of characters that says something the shell could do; it changes nothing, and I have no way to know what would happen if it ran. Executing is the harness actually running that string in a real process with real filesystem, network, and GPU state, then returning output. The key asymmetry: generation is cheap, reversible, and purely textual, while execution is side-effectful, may be irreversible (deletes, network writes), and can produce results I never predicted — so my workflow is generate → inspect → execute → observe, with the boundary between the two owned by the tool, not by me.

Try a question that needs live data

What's NVIDIA stock price today?
Expected output of the agent should be

Expected output: The model should explain that it cannot check today's stock price without live data access. Any price it gives is unverified.

Now connect this to the three terms: Qwen is the model. Open WebUI here provides the conversation interface, but not an action-taking agent workflow. Next, OpenCode is the harness that gives Qwen tools and a work loop; Paseo and VS Code are interfaces for interacting with that agent.

2.2 Paseo: interact with the agent

Paseo is the interface where you chat with the agent while keeping lab instructions and files open. In this lab, it connects to OpenCode running local Qwen; Paseo itself is neither the model nor the harness.

Think of it as a workspace-style interface, similar in spirit to Claude Cowork or the Codex app. Paseo can also connect to Claude Code and Codex when those agents are installed and authenticated.

Paseo supports multiple agents in parallel, voice input, and access from your phone: you can send tasks and check progress while the agents keep running on the connected machine. See the Paseo website for more features.

2.3 VS Code: work with code and files (optional)

On the landing page, click Open VS Code. VS Code provides the editor, file explorer, and terminal. OpenCode runs in the terminal; it is the same harness used through Paseo, not a different model or a separate experiment environment.

From the VS Code web terminal, run:

cd /workspace
./start_opencode.sh

3. Lab architecture

Now since we are in a harness and we've already exposed all the files, including how this lab was built, you can actually ask your agent, "How was this lab built?" Something like

Please read the folders you are in, especially the Docker Compose, and explain to me how this lab was built.
Expected output of the agent should be

You should be getting an answer explaining, like the one below here, how everything is put together. Please ask more follow-up questions to your agent.

Browser
  |
  v
nginx gateway (:80)
  |-- VS Code terminal -> OpenCode ----> miagent container (CPU control plane)
  |-- Paseo browser chat -> OpenCode --> same workspace and agent tools
  |                                         | reads/writes /workspace
  |                                         | reads /data
  |                                         | calls Qwen at llm:8000/v1
  |                                         | submits admitted jobs
  |                                         v
  |                                      training container (GPU science)
  |                                         | PyTorch + MONAI
  |                                         | reads /data
  |                                         | writes challenge artifacts
  |-- MIAgent reports and NiiVue
  |-- MLflow and TensorBoard -----------> tracking container
  `-- browser chat ---------------------> chat container -----> local Qwen

The persistent services have distinct jobs:

Service Purpose
gateway The nginx entry point and only published host port; access is protected by Brev.
miagent VS Code, OpenCode, instructions, tools, reports, and job submission. It is not a CUDA training environment.
training The scientific GPU environment containing PyTorch, MONAI, and the datasets mounted at /data.
paseo Browser interface for interacting with the OpenCode agent.
tracking MLflow and TensorBoard.
llm The local Qwen model behind a private OpenAI-compatible API.
chat Open WebUI for direct browser conversations with the model.

4. Why this separation matters
  • Training dependencies and GPU jobs belong in the training container, not the control container. This is an operational separation, not a security sandbox against an agent with Docker access.
  • The training container can be restarted independently of OpenCode.
  • One fixed dataset is shared without allowing an experiment to edit it.
  • Durable experiment evidence lives in files even when the OpenCode session is reset.
  • The local LLM remains loaded while training runs, so GPU admission must account for both workloads.

The model's context window is its working memory: the prompt, conversation, instructions, file contents, and command output available in a request. It is not permanent memory. Important facts and results must still be written to the challenge files.

5. Skills Available

Ask your agent:

What tools and skills are available to you?
Expected output of the agent should be

In a read-only test, local Qwen returned the following inventory, summarized here:

  • Harness tools: file reading (read), file discovery (glob), content search (grep), skill loading, and web fetching. Tool use depends on the session's permissions.
  • Workflow and compute: challenge orchestration in skills/orchestration/challenge_run_workflow.md, plus Docker, cluster, and GPU guidance in skills/compute/.
  • Data handling: DICOM preflight, metadata extraction, and conversion to volumes in skills/general/.
  • Medical imaging: segmentation skills in skills/segmentation/, synthetic imaging in skills/generation/, chest X-ray reasoning in skills/vlm/, and library guidance in skills/monai/.
  • Helper scripts: environment checks, experiment tracking, segmentation review, and inference publishing in tools/.

Repository skills are instructions and scripts, not necessarily registered OpenCode tools. A documented skill does not guarantee its dependencies or model weights are ready. The agent should check those before executing a task.

Take a minute to ask deeper questions about anything you didn't understand or would like to understand better. Here are some ideas:

  • What is MONAI?
  • What skills do you have for working with MONAI?
  • What algorithms do you have for segmentation?
  • What other skills and model architectures are available to you?
  • What kinds of medical imaging problems can you tackle?

6. Inference Using NV-Segment-CT

Inference uses a pretrained model to predict labels for a new image, without training a new model. Let's explore the NVIDIA segmentation models available through the lab's skills.

6.0 Check model readiness

As part of the lab setup, NV-Segment-CT downloads in the background after the lab starts. Ask your agent to run this check to see whether the model has finished downloading and passed validation:

Check whether the inference model is ready by running:
docker compose -f /workspace/docker-compose.yml exec -T miagent python3 /workspace/tools/prepare_lab_models.py --status
If you are already inside the miagent container, run python3 /workspace/tools/prepare_lab_models.py --status directly instead.

Expected output of the agent should be

The agent should report the status returned by the lab's readiness script, not assume the download has finished:

  • ready: the model has downloaded and passed validation. You can run inference.
  • preparing: downloading or validation is still in progress. Continue the lab and check again later.
  • failed: preparation failed. Ask the agent to explain the reported error and let your instructor know.
  • not_started: no preparation status is available. Let your instructor know.

6.1 Compare the models

Ask your agent:

What is the difference between NV-Segment-CT and NV-Segment-CTMR?
Expected output of the agent should be

They're two different NVIDIA models wrapped by thin skills:

nv-segment-ctnv-segment-ctmr
ModalityCT onlyCT or MRI (CT_BODY, MRI_BODY, MRI_BRAIN)
Upstreamnvidia/NV-Segment-CT (VISTA3D via HuggingFace pipeline)NVIDIA-Medtech/NV-Segment-CTMR (MONAI bundle, model.pt)
Segmentation modeLabel-prompt driven — you request specific VISTA3D class IDs (e.g. liver/spleen/kidneys = 1,3,5,14)Default is per-modality "segment everything"; --label-prompts for a subset
Setup~832 MB HF bundle downloadGit-clone MONAI bundle + model download
CaveatAbdominal CT anatomiesMRI_BRAIN needs upstream brain preprocessing first

Same accuracy? No basis to claim that. Neither SKILL.md publishes Dice/accuracy numbers for its model, so there's no documented comparison in this repo. They are different checkpoints of VISTA3D-lineage foundation models, so even on CT their per-organ results can differ; for MRI only the CTMR skill applies at all.

If you need a quantitative answer, run both on the same volumes with --ground-truth PATH — both skills record the reference map and leave Dice/IoU to the paired verifier (verifiers/ct_segmentation_quality_v1 for CT-body outputs).

6.2 Explore the available data

Search under /data and tell me what kinds of data you have access to, where they are stored, and which datasets are available for inference.
Expected output of the agent should be

The prepared lab provides two CT datasets: /data/ImageCAS_lab and /data/ImageCHD_lab. They are mounted read-only. The agent should inspect the available cases and dataset descriptions rather than assume what is present.

It can also inspect your workspace files and results. Challenge work is saved under /workspace/challenge, and inference predictions under /workspace/inference_tmp. These are outputs, not additional source datasets.

6.3 Run inference

The inference model downloads in the background after the lab starts. If your agent says it is still preparing, continue exploring and try again when it is ready.

Start with one patient:

Run NV-Segment-CT inference using your skill on just one patient from the CAS dataset.

When the patient finishes, follow section 6.4 to inspect its prediction.

After checking the first result, run it on all available CAS patients:

Run NV-Segment-CT inference using your skill on all available patients in the CAS dataset.

6.4 View the predictions

Open Lab Data and Results in a new tab to view the predictions.

Expand inference_tmp, open a patient's result folder, and select result_viewer.html to inspect the image and prediction overlays. Repeat for the other patients as their results become available.
